name: tips.json
description: Basic tips and recommendations for AWS findings

recommendations.name: tops-rec-001
recommendations.impact: Potential data breach or unauthorized access to data
recommendations.description: S3 Buckets should be secured to prevent unauthorized access
steps: Enable S3 Public Access Block
Enable S3 Bucket Encryption

recommendations.name: tops-rec-002
recommendations.description: EC2 Instances to be secured to limit access to systems. This should include disabling IAM Roles and Public IP Addresses
steps: Remove Public IP Address
Remove or reduce IAM Role Instance Profile permissions
Add an optional Load Balancer to provide access to the instance from outside the VPC

recommendations.name: tops-rec-003
recommendations.impact: Potential outage not detected or recovered from
recommendations.description: EC2 Instances to enable Cloudwatch Monitoring to detect potential outages and enable Auto Recovery to recover from them
steps: Enable Cloudwatch Monitoring
Enable Auto Recovery

recommendations.name: tops-rec-004
recommendations.description: IAM Users must have an MFA device enabled
steps: Enable MFA for IAM Users

recommendations.name: tops-rec-005
recommendations.description: IAM Users should not have access keys
steps: Remove IAM User Access Keys
Use AWS Cloud Shell
Use AWS CLI V2 and enable authentication through IAM Identity Center

recommendations.name: tops-rec-006
recommendations.description: VPC Subnets should be secured to prevent unauthorized access
steps: Set Default EC2 Instances to Private IP Address only
Ensure subnets with EC2 instances have a private route table

recommendations.name: tops-rec-007
recommendations.description: IAM Policies to be managed through IAM Groups
steps: Setup IAM Group
Add IAM Policies to IAM Group
Add Users to IAM Group
Remove IAM Policies from IAM User

recommendations.name: tops-rec-009
recommendations.impact: Full, unrestricted control of the AWS account. Root cannot be scoped down by any policy, and its actions cannot be prevented — only detected afterwards.
recommendations.description: The root user should have MFA enabled and no access keys. Day-to-day work belongs to IAM users and roles.
steps: Sign in as root and open My Security Credentials
Delete every key listed under Access keys — nothing should be using them
Choose Assign MFA device and register a hardware key or authenticator app
Store the MFA recovery method where more than one person can reach it
Create an IAM user or role with scoped permissions for the work root was doing
Set a CloudWatch alarm on root sign-in so future use is noticed

recommendations.name: tops-rec-010
recommendations.recommendation: Remove administrative permissions from IAM users
recommendations.impact: One stolen credential becomes a full account compromise. Standing admin also removes any audit signal that a privileged action was intended.
recommendations.description: Users should hold only the permissions their work needs, granted through groups rather than attached directly.
steps: List what the user actually calls: IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from their recent CloudTrail activity
Create a customer managed policy from that, or start from a narrow AWS managed policy rather than one ending in FullAccess
Put the policy on a group and add the user to it
Detach AdministratorAccess, any *FullAccess policy, and any inline policy using '*'
If admin is genuinely required, make it a role the user assumes deliberately instead of standing access

recommendations.name: tops-rec-011
recommendations.recommendation: Stop S3 buckets being publicly readable
recommendations.impact: Anyone on the internet can list and download objects. Most large data exposures are a bucket nobody meant to leave open.
recommendations.description: Buckets should have Block Public Access fully enabled and no public ACL grants.
steps: Check first whether anything legitimately serves public content from this bucket
S3 > bucket > Permissions > Access control list: remove grants to Everyone and to Authenticated users
S3 > bucket > Permissions > Block public access: enable all four settings
Enable Block Public Access at the account level so new buckets inherit it
For content that must be public, put CloudFront in front with an origin access control and keep the bucket private

recommendations.name: tops-rec-012
recommendations.impact: Snapshots, storage volumes and backups are readable by anyone who obtains them. Encryption cannot be added later without a migration.
recommendations.description: RDS instances and clusters should have encryption at rest enabled. It cannot be toggled on an existing database.
steps: Take a snapshot of the instance or cluster
Copy the snapshot, ticking Enable encryption and choosing a KMS key
Restore a new database from the encrypted copy
Repoint the application and verify it reads and writes correctly
Delete the unencrypted original and its snapshots only once the new one is confirmed

recommendations.name: tops-rec-013
recommendations.recommendation: Take databases off the public internet
recommendations.impact: The database is reachable from any address, leaving only its password between an attacker and the data.
recommendations.description: RDS instances should not be publicly accessible; reach them from inside the VPC.
steps: Identify what currently connects from outside the VPC before changing anything
RDS > database > Modify > Connectivity: set Public access to No
Restrict the security group to the application's security group rather than a CIDR range
For human access use Session Manager port forwarding, a VPN, or a bastion host

recommendations.name: tops-rec-014
recommendations.recommendation: Close administrative ports to the internet
recommendations.impact: SSH and RDP open to 0.0.0.0/0 are scanned and brute-forced continuously, within minutes of being exposed.
recommendations.description: No security group or network ACL should allow 0.0.0.0/0 to reach port 22 or 3389.
steps: Find the offending rules: EC2 > Security Groups, and VPC > Network ACLs
Replace 0.0.0.0/0 with the specific ranges that need administrative access
Better: remove inbound SSH and RDP entirely and use Systems Manager Session Manager, which needs no open port and logs every session
Empty the default security group of every VPC so nothing uses it by accident
Remember network ACLs are stateless — return traffic needs a matching outbound rule

recommendations.name: tops-rec-015
recommendations.recommendation: Make CloudTrail a reliable audit record
recommendations.impact: Without a complete, tamper-evident trail there is no way to reconstruct what happened during an incident — and no way to prove what did not happen.
recommendations.description: CloudTrail should be logging in all regions, with log file validation on and delivery to CloudWatch Logs.
steps: CloudTrail > Trails: create a trail with Apply trail to all regions enabled, or edit the existing one
Confirm logging is actually started — a trail can exist and be stopped
Enable log file validation so tampering can be detected afterwards
Send the trail to CloudWatch Logs so you can alarm on activity instead of reading logs later
Encrypt the trail with a KMS customer managed key, allowing CloudTrail to encrypt and your readers to decrypt

recommendations.name: tops-rec-016
recommendations.impact: IMDSv1 lets a server-side request forgery bug in an application read the instance's IAM role credentials — the standard path from a web vulnerability to AWS access.
recommendations.description: Instance metadata should require session tokens (IMDSv2) rather than allowing unauthenticated IMDSv1 requests.
steps: Check your SDK versions first — anything current speaks IMDSv2, but very old SDKs and hand-rolled metadata calls do not
EC2 > instance > Actions > Instance settings > Modify instance metadata options
Set IMDSv2 to Required
Set the hop limit to 1 unless the workload is containerised, in which case 2
Bake the same setting into launch templates and AMIs so new instances inherit it

recommendations.name: tops-rec-017
recommendations.impact: A function URL with no authentication is a public endpoint. Anyone who finds it can invoke the function and be billed to your account.
recommendations.description: Lambda function URLs should use AWS_IAM auth, unless the endpoint is deliberately public.
steps: Confirm whether this endpoint is meant to be public
Lambda > function > Configuration > Function URL > Edit: set Auth type to AWS_IAM
Grant lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl to the specific callers that need it
If it must stay public, put API Gateway or CloudFront in front so you get throttling and WAF

recommendations.name: tops-rec-018
recommendations.recommendation: Review KMS keys scheduled for deletion
recommendations.impact: When the key is deleted, everything encrypted with it becomes permanently unreadable. There is no recovery afterwards — only the waiting period.
recommendations.description: A key pending deletion should be confirmed as genuinely unused before the window elapses.
steps: KMS > customer managed keys: note the scheduled deletion date
Check CloudTrail for recent Decrypt and GenerateDataKey calls against the key
Look for encrypted resources still referencing it — EBS volumes, RDS snapshots, S3 buckets, Secrets Manager secrets
If anything still depends on it, choose Cancel key deletion immediately
If it is genuinely unused, record why it was deleted before the window closes
